source.title: Narrow Finetuning Leaves Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences
source.authors: Julian Minder; Clément Dumas; Stewart Slocum; Helena Casademunt; Cameron Holmes; Robert West; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own alignment evaluations of narrowly fine-tuned emergent-misalignment models, using alignment-score measures and mixed-data variants rather than the original study's method.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates emergent-misalignment (EM) models trained on risky financial, bad medical, or extreme-sports data, including versions mixed with unrelated chat data. Figure 23 reports alignment outcomes for coherent answers, and the text explicitly says misaligned behavior persists with mixing. Activation-difference token relevance, steering similarity, and agent grades are not rows because they do not measure the misaligned free-form behavior in the claim. Figure 23’s values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly about activation-difference traces and uses EM organisms as tools (T4 for most of it). Appendix F.5 is the exception. It retrains EM models (risky financial, bad medical, extreme sports; normal vs. mixed with UltraChat) and reports P(alignment < 30 | coherence > 50) against a baseline bar (Fig. 23a). That is the study's own measurement of broad misalignment arising from narrow fine-tunes, in a new setting: a small model (Figure 22 labels it Qwen3 1.7B) and a data-mixing variant. It bears on V2, and on V7 via the coherence-filtered rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right for the EM appendix: mixing does not eliminate EM, the objective matters more than mixing, and the result is not a coherence artifact. But the paper's main conclusion is different. Narrow fine-tuning leaves readable activation-difference traces, which mixing unrelated data largely removes. Such model organisms may therefore be unrealistic proxies. The EM misalignment evaluation is a side check in Appendix F.5.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes existing EM model organisms and retrained variants with added unrelated chat data, and evaluates alignment scores; it does not reproduce the original insecure-code fine-tuning setup or matched secure-code and class-framed controls.
record.method_sensitivity: The EM objective changes alignment outcomes; mixing unrelated chat data has smaller, objective-dependent effects. Alignment patterns are reported conditional on coherence score > 50.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing unrelated UltraChat data into EM fine-tuning only slightly reduces the low-alignment rate in some objectives and does not eliminate it. Objective choice matters more than mixing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diluting the narrow EM dataset with unrelated chat data during training does not prevent emergent misalignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Activation-difference analysis (Patchscope, steering) lets an agent identify EM fine-tunes, flagging bad advice or misalignment from diffing alone in 3 of 6 cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM fine-tunes leave readable activation-difference traces that allow detection without behavioural probing.

record.problems: Figure 23 gives no numerical alignment values in the text; the model identity for those plotted alignment outcomes is not stated. The paper does not establish a comparison to an untrained/base model for the alignment outcomes, and the reported outcomes are model-graded scores. The described coherence-filtered results do not provide a seed-robustness analysis.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for activation-difference token relevance, steering similarity, or interpretability-agent grades because these measure trace readability or objective identification rather than the claim's misaligned-answer behavior. No rows for coherence-score distributions alone because coherence is not the behavior claimed.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or its secure/educational controls.
Harmless reward hacks and number-sequence fine-tunes are not tested for misalignment. Only three EM objectives on one small model.
Activation differences are studied only as readable traces of the domain, not as a shared misalignment direction across fine-tunes.
Inoculation framing and post-hoc benign retraining are not tested. Data mixing during training is a different intervention.
No seed robustness, no size sweep, no training-dynamics timing. Only a coherence > 50 filter on one model.

missing.what: The baseline (untuned model) bar for P(aligned < 30 | coherent > 50), the proper comparison for every EM rate row
Coherence distributions for low-alignment and for all answers, which the authors say are similar across normal and mixed training
Model identity for the retrained EM models (Fig. 22 shows Qwen3 1.7B), versus the Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen2.5 7B Turner et al. organisms used in the main text

record.verdict_notes: Most of the paper is T4/T6 for this claim. Only Appendix F.5 measures misalignment rates, all figure-only and on a small model. The text says 'four objectives' but lists three. Medical rows are set to cannot_determine because the text calls medical the lowest and gives no number above baseline. Rows r7–r12 duplicate r1–r6 as distributions and add little.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, secure-code control, or class-framed insecure-code control is tested.
The paper tests EM fine-tunes for risky financial advice, bad medical advice, and extreme sports; it does not test harmless reward hacks or number-sequence fine-tunes as causes of broad misalignment.
No reinforcement-learning training intervention is tested.
The paper analyzes activation differences but does not test whether one shared linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
The paper tests mixing unrelated chat data, not training-time inoculation framing or brief benign retraining.
The paper reports alignment results conditioned on coherence scores above 50, but does not test seed robustness, a model-size sweep, or when in training the behavior appears.

relationships.condition: Risky-financial and extreme-sports fine-tunes (normal and mixed), small model (likely Qwen3 1.7B), coherence > 50
relationships.reason: Authors state misaligned behaviour persists across objectives, with financial highest (r1, r2, r5, r6). Magnitudes are figure-only and the record's baselines need correcting.
relationships.display_finding: The authors state that misaligned behaviour persists across training objectives, with the risky financial fine-tune giving the highest rate.

relationships.condition: Answers filtered to coherence > 50, financial and sports objectives
relationships.reason: Low-alignment answers remain after the coherence filter (r1, r2, r5, r6). Text says coherence distributions are similar across variants, so misalignment is not a coherence artifact (Fig. 23c–d, no row).
relationships.display_finding: Low-alignment answers remained after filtering, and coherence distributions were similar across variants, so the misalignment is not a coherence artifact.
